3. The first contention regarding the applicant is that whether applicant comes within the definition of 
workman as is defined in Section 2(s) of the Act. I may mention that applicant was appointed as sweeper as per his 
claim petition and affidavit submitted before the Tribunal. In plain words the applicant was performing his duties as 
labourer/unskilled worker. He was not in supervisory or administrative post requiring him to perform only 
administrative duties. While interpreting Section 2(s) Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Devinder Singh Vs. 
Municipal Council, Sanaur, AIR 20I] Supreme Court 2532,has observed as follows:- 


“The source of employment, the quantum of recruitment, the terms & conditions of employment contract of 
service, the quantum of wages/ pay and mode of payment are not at all relevant for deciding whether or not a 
person is a workman within the meaning of Section 2(s) of the Act. The definition of workman also does not 
make any distinction between full time and part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. 
There is nothing in the plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be inferred that only person 
employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one 
employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty 
for fixed hours is not a workman.” 


4. Thus Hon’ble Supreme Court has clarified that the definition of workman also does not make any distinction 
between full time or part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is nothing in plain language of 
Section 2(s) from which it can be infer that only person employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing 
whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a 
casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a workman. In view of the ratio of law enunciated in the 
above ruling, in my considered opinion the applicant herein admittedly falls within the definition of ‘workman’ under 
Section 2(s) of the Act.

India Limited in Civil Appeal ४०.70266 dated 25.08, 207/4, two well recognized tests to find out whether the labours 
are the contract employees of the principal employer are:- 


3) Whether the principal employer pays the salary instead of contractor and

Moreover, workman is not employee of respondent no.| being employee of respondent no.2 (contractor).

Findings:- 

3. The first contention regarding the applicant is that whether applicant comes within the definition of 
workman as is defined in Section 2(s) of the Act. I may mention that applicant was appointed as sweeper as per his 
claim petition and affidavit submitted before the Tribunal. In plain words the applicant was performing his duties as 
labourer/unskilled worker. He was not in supervisory or administrative post requiring him to perform only 
administrative duties. While interpreting Section 2(s) Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Devinder Singh Vs. 
Municipal Council, Sanaur, AIR 20I] Supreme Court 2532,has observed as follows:- 


“The source of employment, the quantum of recruitment, the terms & conditions of employment/ contract of 
service, the quantum of wages/ pay and mode of payment are not at all relevant for deciding whether or not a 
person is a workman within the meaning of Section 2(s) of the Act. The definition of workman also does not 
make any distinction between full time and part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. 
There is nothing in the plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be inferred that only person 
employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one 
employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty 
for fixed hours is not a workman.” 


4. Thus Hon’ble Supreme Court has clarified that the definition of workman also does not make any distinction 
between full time or part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is nothing in plain language of 
Section 2(s) from which it can be infer that only person employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing 
whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a 
casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a workman. In view of the ratio of law enunciated in the 
above ruling, in my considered opinion the applicant herein admittedly falls within the definition of ‘workman’ under 
Section 2(s) of the Act. 


5. The Hon’ble Supreme Court after analyzing the catena of cases has laid down in Balwant Raj Saluja Vs. Air 
India Limited in Civil Appeal ५०. 70266 dated 25.08.204, two well recognized tests to find out whether the labours 
are the contract employees of the principal employer are:- 


3) Whether the principal employer pays the salary instead of contractor and 
2) Whether the principal employer controls and supervise the work of the employees?

petition of the workman. In fact, claim petition is totally silent regarding the payment of wages, salary, letter of 
appointment by respondent no.| or by contractor or anything likewise. Thus, this basic feature for holding the 
relationship of employer and employee i.e. between respondent no.! and workman totally lacking not in the pleading 
but also in the evidence submitted by the workman.However, MWI Colonel K P Singh in his cross examination has 
stated that it is responsibility of the contractor to pay monthly wages to the conservancy staff provided by him. 
Respondent no.! has nothing to do with the minimum wages, DC rate to the conservancy staff. Contractor is 
responsible to give notice to the conservancy staff provided by him. Respondent no.! has no roll in terminating the 
services of the workman. Thus, it was the respondent no.2 who was required to ensure the payment of wages to the 
workers engaged by him from time to time.

the contract agreement between respondent no.| & 2. Thus, from the adduced evidence, it emerges that workman was 
paid salary by the contractor and he was being controlled and supervised by the contractor. Thus, there does not exist 
any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.l. However, there exists relation 
of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.2. 


8. It is also added here that as per definition of contractor as given in the Section 2(c) of the Contract Labour 
(Regulation and Abolition) Act, 970 (hereinafter called as Contract Act), respondent no.2 was supplying contract 
labour to the respondent no.l. Thus, respondent no.2 would fall under the definition of contractor. Section 2(c) of the 
Contract Act is reproduced as under: 


“Contractor”, in relation to an establishment, means a person who undertakes to produce a given result for the 
establishment, other than a mere supply of goods or articles of manufacture to such establishment, through contract 
labour or who supplies contract labour for any work of the establishment and includes a sub-contractor; 


9. TheHon’ble Apex Court in the case of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board Vs. A. Rajappa /928(36) 
FLR 266 dealt at length with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in Section 2(j) of the Act, and

has laid down triple test for determining whether a particular establishment is industry or not. The triple test is where 
(a) systematic activity (b) organized by cooperation between employer and employee (the direct and substantial 
element is commercial (c) for the production or distribution of goods and services to calculated to satisfy human 
wants and wishes prima facie is an “Industry” in that enterprise. The workman was doing work i.e. systematic activity 
for respondent no.| at the asking of respondent no.2 and there was cooperation between the workman and respondent 
no.2, which involve substantial commercial element for rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, respondent 
no.2 would be termed as industry.

the Act. He also stated that he was appointed on 0!.04.207 and he was paid minimum wages prescribed by Central 
Government and was working with respondent no.l. He was not given any compensation before terminating his 
services on 27.!0.208. In his cross examination, he has further stated that his salary used to be credited in his bank 
account. But he has not placed on record any bank account, in which his salary was credited in order to enable this 
Court to see who was making payment to the workman. However, there is no denial that the workman was paid salary 
by respondent no.2 (contractor). However, from the agreement dated 05.07.20I8 (Ex.R-2) placed on file by 
respondent no.l, it emerges that safai karamcharis were provided by respondent no.2 (contractor) to work with 
respondent no.l. Thus, workman was employee of respondent no.2 and not of respondent no.! as has been discussed 
above. There does not exist any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.|. 
However, there exists relation of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.2. 


2I. Admittedly, there is non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2. However, as regards 
violation of other provisions i.e. Section 25G and 25H of the Act, there is no evidence lead by the workman. Hence, 
workman is entitled for compensation from respondent no.2.

by entering into contract with contractors for supply of safai karamcharis and agreement executed between 
respondent no.! and 2 cannot be said to be any unfair labour practice. So far as contentions of AR for workman that

3. The first contention regarding the applicant is that whether applicant comes within the definition of 
workman as is defined in Section 2(s) of the Act. I may mention that applicant was appointed as sweeper as per his 
claim petition and affidavit submitted before the Tribunal. In plain words the applicant was performing his duties as 
labourer/unskilled worker. He was not in supervisory or administrative post requiring him to perform only 
administrative duties. While interpreting Section 2(s) Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Devinder Singh Vs.

person is a workman within the meaning of Section 2(s) of the Act. The definition of workman also does not 
make any distinction between full time and part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. 
There is nothing in the plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be inferred that only person 
employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one 
employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty 
for fixed hours is not a workman.”

between full time or part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is nothing in plain language of 
Section 2(s) from which it can be infer that only person employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing 
whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a 
casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a workman. In view of the ratio of law enunciated in the 
above ruling, in my considered opinion the applicant herein admittedly falls within the definition of ‘workman’ under 
Section 2(s) of the Act.

India Limited in Civil Appeal ५०. 70266 dated 25.08, 20/4, two well recognized tests to find out whether the labours

has laid down triple test for determining whether a particular establishment is industry or not. The triple test is where

(a) systematic activity (b) organized by cooperation between employer and employee (the direct and substantial

wants and wishes prima facie is an “Industry” in that enterprise. The workman was doing work i.e. systematic activity 
for respondent no.| at the asking of respondent no.2 and there was cooperation between the workman and respondent 
no.2, which involve substantial commercial element for rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, respondent 
no.2 would be termed as industry.

violation of other provisions i.e. Section 25G and 25H of the Act, there is no evidence lead by the workman. Hence,

Findings:- 
3. The first contention regarding the applicant is that whether applicant comes within the definition of workman 


as is defined in Section 2(s) of the Act. I may mention that applicant was appointed as sweeper as per his claim 
petition and affidavit submitted before the Tribunal. In plain words the applicant was performing his duties as 


4276 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MAY 6, 2026/VAISAKHA 26, 948 [Part II—SECc. 3(ii)] 


labourer/unskilled worker. He was not in supervisory or administrative post requiring him to perform only 
administrative duties. While interpreting Section 2(s) Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Devinder Singh Vs. 


Municipal Council, Sanaur, AIR 20I] Supreme Court 2532,has observed as follows:- 


“The source of employment, the quantum of recruitment, the terms & conditions of employment/ contract of 
service, the quantum of wages/ pay and mode of payment are not at all relevant for deciding whether or not a 
person is a workman within the meaning of Section 2(s) of the Act. The definition of workman also does not 
make any distinction between full time and part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. 
There is nothing in the plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be inferred that only person 
employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one 
employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty 
for fixed hours is not a workman.” 


4. Thus Hon’ble Supreme Court has clarified that the definition of workman also does not make any distinction 
between full time or part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is nothing in plain language of 
Section 2(s) from which it can be infer that only person employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing 
whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a 
casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a workman. In view of the ratio of law enunciated in the 
above ruling, in my considered opinion the applicant herein admittedly falls within the definition of ‘workman’ under 
Section 2(s) of the Act. 


5. The Hon’ble Supreme Court after analyzing the catena of cases has laid down in Balwant Raj Saluja Vs. Air 
India Limited in Civil Appeal ५७०.70266 dated 25.06. 20/4, two well recognized tests to find out whether the labours 
are the contract employees of the principal employer are:- 


3) Whether the principal employer pays the salary instead of contractor and 
2) Whether the principal employer controls and supervise the work of the employees? 


6. The facts regarding the payment of salary by the management or contractor has not been stated in the claim 
petition of the workman. In fact, claim petition is totally silent regarding the payment of wages, salary, letter of 
appointment by respondent no.! or by contractor or anything likewise. Thus, this basic feature for holding the 
relationship of employer and employee i.e. between respondent no.! and workman totally lacking not in the pleading 
but also in the evidence submitted by the workman.However, MWI Colonel K P Singh in his cross examination has 
stated that it is responsibility of the contractor to pay monthly wages to the conservancy staff provided by him. 
Respondent no.l has nothing to do with the minimum wages, DC rate to the conservancy staff. Contractor is 
responsible to give notice to the conservancy staff provided by him. Respondent no.! has no roll in terminating the 
services of the workman. Thus, it was the respondent no.2 who was required to ensure the payment of wages to the 
workers engaged by him from time to time. 


7. It is also added here that respondent no.! has also placed on record documents Ex.R-| to Ex.R-4. Ex.R-2 is 
the contract agreement between respondent no.| & 2. Thus, from the adduced evidence, it emerges that workman was 
paid salary by the contractor and he was being controlled and supervised by the contractor. Thus, there does not exist 
any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.l. However, there exists relation 
of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.2. 


8. It is also added here that as per definition of contractor as given in the Section 2(c) of the Contract Labour 
(Regulation and Abolition) Act, 970 (hereinafter called as Contract Act), respondent no.2 was supplying contract 
labour to the respondent no.!. Thus, respondent no.2 would fall under the definition of contractor. Section 2(c) of the 
Contract Act is reproduced as under: 


“Contractor”, in relation to an establishment, means a person who undertakes to produce a given result for the 
establishment, other than a mere supply of goods or articles of manufacture to such establishment, through contract 
labour or who supplies contract labour for any work of the establishment and includes a sub-contractor; 


9. TheHon’ble Apex Court in the case of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board Vs. A. Rajappa /०78(36) 
FLR 266 dealt at length with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in Section 2(j) of the Act, and 


has laid down triple test for determining whether a particular establishment is industry or not. The triple test is where 
(a) systematic activity (b) organized by cooperation between employer and employee (the direct and substantial 
element is commercial (c) for the production or distribution of goods and services to calculated to satisfy human 
wants and wishes prima facie is an “Industry” in that enterprise. The workman was doing work i.e. systematic activity 
for respondent no.| at the asking of respondent no.2 and there was cooperation between the workman and respondent 
no.2, which involve substantial commercial element for rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, respondent 
no.2 would be termed as industry.

However, there exists relation of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.2. 


2]. Admittedly, there is non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2. However, as regards 
violation of other provisions i.e. Section 25G and 25H of the Act, there is no evidence lead by the workman. Hence,

22. It is also added here that there is no iota of evidence that any unfair labour practice used by respondent no.| 
by entering into contract with contractors for supply of safai karamcharis and agreement executed between respondent

not employee of respondent no.! being employee of respondent no.2 (contractor).

period of his stay with the contractor and non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act, this Tribunal is of the considered 
opinion that workman is entitled for compensation.

as is defined in Section 2(s) of the Act. I may mention that applicant was appointed as sweeper as per his claim 
petition and affidavit submitted before the Tribunal. In plain words the applicant was performing his duties as 
labourer/unskilled worker. He was not in supervisory or administrative post requiring him to perform only 
administrative duties. While interpreting Section 2(s) Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Devinder Singh Vs.

Municipal Council, Sanaur, AIR 20I] Supreme Court 2532,has observed as follows:- 


“The source of employment, the quantum of recruitment, the terms & conditions of employment/ contract of 
service, the quantum of wages/ pay and mode of payment are not at all relevant for deciding whether or not a 
person is a workman within the meaning of Section 2(s) of the Act. The definition of workman also does not 
make any distinction between full time and part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. 
There is nothing in the plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be inferred that only person 
employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one 
employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty 
for fixed hours is not a workman.” 


4. Thus Hon’ble Supreme Court has clarified that the definition of workman also does not make any distinction 
between full time or part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is nothing in plain language of 
Section 2(s) from which it can be infer that only person employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing 
whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a 
casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a workman. In view of the ratio of law enunciated in the 
above ruling, in my considered opinion the applicant herein admittedly falls within the definition of ‘workman’ under 
Section 2(s) of the Act. 


5. The Hon’ble Supreme Court after analyzing the catena of cases has laid down in Balwant Raj Saluja Vs. Air 
India Limited in Civil Appeal ५७०.70266 dated 25.06. 20/4, two well recognized tests to find out whether the labours 
are the contract employees of the principal employer are:- 


3) Whether the principal employer pays the salary instead of contractor and 
2) Whether the principal employer controls and supervise the work of the employees? 


6. The facts regarding the payment of salary by the management or contractor has not been stated in the claim 
petition of the workman. In fact, claim petition is totally silent regarding the payment of wages, salary, letter of 
appointment by respondent no.l or by contractor or anything likewise. Thus, this basic feature for holding the 
relationship of employer and employee i.e. between respondent no.! and workman totally lacking not in the pleading 
but also in the evidence submitted by the workman.However, ४७] Colonel K P Singh in his cross examination has 
stated that it is responsibility of the contractor to pay monthly wages to the conservancy staff provided by him. 
Respondent no.l has nothing to do with the minimum wages, DC rate to the conservancy staff. Contractor is 
responsible to give notice to the conservancy staff provided by him. Respondent no.! has no roll in terminating the 
services of the workman. Thus, it was the respondent no.2 who was required to ensure the payment of wages to the 
workers engaged by him from time to time. 


7. It is also added here that respondent no.! has also placed on record documents Ex.R-| to Ex.R-4. Ex.R-2 is 
the contract agreement between respondent no.| & 2. Thus, from the adduced evidence, it emerges that workman was 
paid salary by the contractor and he was being controlled and supervised by the contractor. Thus, there does not exist 
any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.l. However, there exists relation 
of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.2. 


8. It is also added here that as per definition of contractor as given in the Section 2(c) of the Contract Labour 
(Regulation and Abolition) Act, 970 (hereinafter called as Contract Act), respondent no.2 was supplying contract 
labour to the respondent no.!. Thus, respondent no.2 would fall under the definition of contractor. Section 2(c) of the 
Contract Act is reproduced as under: 


“Contractor”, in relation to an establishment, means a person who undertakes to produce a given result for the 
establishment, other than a mere supply of goods or articles of manufacture to such establishment, through contract 
labour or who supplies contract labour for any work of the establishment and includes a sub-contractor; 


9. TheHon’ble Apex Court in the case of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board Vs. A. Rajappa /9०78(36) 
FLR 266 dealt at length with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in Section 2(j) of the Act, and 


has laid down triple test for determining whether a particular establishment is industry or not. The triple test is where 
(a) systematic activity (b) organized by cooperation between employer and employee (the direct and substantial 
element is commercial (c) for the production or distribution of goods and services to calculated to satisfy human 
wants and wishes prima facie is an “Industry” in that enterprise. The workman was doing work i.e. systematic activity 
for respondent no.|! at the asking of respondent no.2 and there was cooperation between the workman and respondent 
no.2, which involve substantial commercial element for rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, respondent 
no.2 would be termed as industry.

the Act. He also stated that he was appointed on 0!.04.204 and he was paid minimum wages prescribed by Central 
Government and was working with respondent no.l. He was not given any compensation before terminating his 
services on 27.0.208. In his cross examination, he has further stated that his salary used to be credited in his bank 
account. But he has not placed on record any bank account, in which his salary was credited in order to enable this 
Court to see who was making payment to the workman. However, there is no denial that the workman was paid salary 
by respondent no.2 (contractor). However, from the agreement dated 05.07.20I8 (Ex.R-2) placed on file by

respondent no.l, it emerges that safai karamcharis were provided by respondent no.2 (contractor) to work with 
respondent no.l. Thus, workman was employee of respondent no.2 and not of respondent no.! as has been discussed 
above. There does not exist any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.|. 
However, there exists relation of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.2.

violation of other provisions i.e. Section 25G and 25H of the Act, there is no evidence lead by the workman. Hence, 
workman is entitled for compensation from respondent no.2.

by entering into contract with contractors for supply of safai karamcharis and agreement executed between respondent 
no.! and 2 cannot be said to be any unfair labour practice. So far as contentions of AR for workman that the work 
performed by the workman is of perennial in nature and no domestic inquiry was held before terminating the services

because work is of perennial in nature does not mean that any right has accrued in favour of the workman to get 
employment with respondent no.l, which is a department of Civil Defence run by Government of India and for that 
regular recruitment procedure is provided. Workman cannot seek backdoor entry into service. Moreover, workman is 
not employee of respondent no.| being employee of respondent no.2 (contractor).

respondent no.|, so keeping in view the tenure of service rendered by the workman and salary given to him during the 
period of his stay with the contractor and non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act, this Tribunal is of the considered 
opinion that workman is entitled for compensation.

deemed fit by this Tribunal: 


i. Workman who worked for less than 2 years with contractor shall be entitled for Rs.20,000/-. 

il. Workman who worked for more than 2 years but less than 5 years with contractor shall be entitled 
Rs.30,000/-. 

ili. Workman who worked for more than 5 years with contractors shall be entitled for Rs.50,000/-. 

25. Present workman employed on 0.04.20i4 and was terminated on 27.0.20l8 (more than 2 years and less 


than 5 years), so he is entitled for Rs.30,000/-.

Findings:- 

3. The first contention regarding the applicant is that whether applicant comes within the definition of 
workman as is defined in Section 2(s) of the Act. I may mention that applicant was appointed as sweeper as per his 
claim petition and affidavit submitted before the Tribunal. In plain words the applicant was performing his duties as 
labourer/unskilled worker. He was not in supervisory or administrative post requiring him to perform only 
administrative duties. While interpreting Section 2(s) Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Devinder Singh Vs. 


Municipal Council, Sanaur, AIR 20I] Supreme Court 2532,has observed as follows:- 


“The source of employment, the quantum of recruitment, the terms & conditions of employment/ contract of 
service, the quantum of wages/ pay and mode of payment are not at all relevant for deciding whether or not a 
person is a workman within the meaning of Section 2(s) of the Act. The definition of workman also does not 
make any distinction between full time and part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. 
There is nothing in the plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be inferred that only person 
employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one 


4288 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MAY 6, 2026/VAISAKHA 26, 948 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty 
for fixed hours is not a workman.” 


4. Thus Hon’ble Supreme Court has clarified that the definition of workman also does not make any distinction 
between full time or part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is nothing in plain language 
of Section 2(s) from which it can be infer that only person employed on regular basis or a person employed for 
doing whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages 
or as a casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a workman. In view of the ratio of law enunciated in 
the above ruling, in my considered opinion the applicant herein admittedly falls within the definition of ‘workman’ 
under Section 2(s) of the Act. 


5. The Hon’ble Supreme Court after analyzing the catena of cases has laid down in Balwant Raj Saluja Vs. Air 
India Limited in Civil Appeal ७०.70266 dated 25.08,.20/4, two well recognized tests to find out whether the 
labours are the contract employees of the principal employer are:- 


3) Whether the principal employer pays the salary instead of contractor and 
2) Whether the principal employer controls and supervise the work of the employees? 


6. The facts regarding the payment of salary by the management or contractor has not been stated in the claim 
petition of the workman. In fact, claim petition is totally silent regarding the payment of wages, salary, letter of 
appointment by respondent no.| or by contractor or anything likewise. Thus, this basic feature for holding the 
relationship of employer and employee i.e. between respondent no.! and workman totally lacking not in the pleading 
but also in the evidence submitted by the workman.However, ५७४] Colonel K P Singh in his cross examination has 
stated that it is responsibility of the contractor to pay monthly wages to the conservancy staff provided by him. 
Respondent no.l has nothing to do with the minimum wages, DC rate to the conservancy staff. Contractor is 
responsible to give notice to the conservancy staff provided by him. Respondent no.! has no roll in terminating the 
services of the workman. Thus, it was the respondent no.2 who was required to ensure the payment of wages to the 
workers engaged by him from time to time. 


7. It is also added here that respondent no.! has also placed on record documents Ex.R-| to Ex.R-4. Ex.R-2 is 
the contract agreement between respondent no.! & 2. Thus, from the adduced evidence, it emerges that workman was 
paid salary by the contractor and he was being controlled and supervised by the contractor. Thus, there does not exist 
any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.|. However, there exists relation 
of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.2. 


8. It is also added here that as per definition of contractor as given in the Section 2(c) of the Contract Labour 
(Regulation and Abolition) Act, 970 (hereinafter called as Contract Act), respondent no.2 was supplying contract 
labour to the respondent no.l. Thus, respondent no.2 would fall under the definition of contractor. Section 2(c) of the 
Contract Act is reproduced as under: 


“Contractor”, in relation to an establishment, means a person who undertakes to produce a given result for the 
establishment, other than a mere supply of goods or articles of manufacture to such establishment, through contract 
labour or who supplies contract labour for any work of the establishment and includes a sub-contractor; 


9. TheHon’ble Apex Court in the case of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board Vs. A. Rajappa /9728(36) 
FLR 266 dealt at length with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in Section 2(j) of the Act, and 


has laid down triple test for determining whether a particular establishment is industry or not. The triple test is where 
(a) systematic activity (b) organized by cooperation between employer and employee (the direct and substantial 
element is commercial (c) for the production or distribution of goods and services to calculated to satisfy human 
wants and wishes prima facie is an “Industry” in that enterprise. The workman was doing work i.e. systematic activity 
for respondent no. at the asking of respondent no.2 and there was cooperation between the workman and respondent 
no.2, which involve substantial commercial element for rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, respondent 
no.2 would be termed as industry. 


20. Workman in his deposition has clearly stated that there was non-compliance of Section 25F, 25G and 25H of 
the Act. He also stated that he was appointed on 0!.09.202 and he was paid minimum wages prescribed by Central 
Government and was working with respondent no.l!. He was not given any compensation before terminating his 
services on 27.!0.208. In his cross examination, he has further stated that his salary used to be credited in his bank 
account. But he has not placed on record any bank account, in which his salary was credited in order to enable this 
Court to see who was making payment to the workman. However, there is no denial that the workman was paid salary 
by respondent no.2 (contractor). However, from the agreement dated 05.07.20I8 (Ex.R-2) placed on file by 
respondent no.l, it emerges that safai karamcharis were provided by respondent no.2 (contractor) to work with 
respondent no.l. Thus, workman was employee of respondent no.2 and not of respondent no.! as has been discussed 
above. There does not exist any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.|. 
However, there exists relation of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no. 2.

2. Admittedly, there is non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2. However, as regards 
violation of other provisions i.e. Section 25G and 25H of the Act, there is no evidence lead by the workman. Hence, 
workman is entitled for compensation from respondent no.2. 


22. It is also added here that there is no iota of evidence that any unfair labour practice used by respondent no. | 
by entering into contract with contractors for supply of safai karamcharis and agreement executed between 
respondent no.! and 2 cannot be said to be any unfair labour practice. So far as contentions of AR for workman that 
the work performed by the workman is of perennial in nature and no domestic inquiry was held before terminating 
the services of workman are concerned, in this regard, it is pointed out that workman was entitled only for 
compensation under Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2 (contractor) and no domestic inquiry was required to 
be conducted. Merely because work is of perennial in nature does not mean that any right has accrued in favour of the 
workman to get employment with respondent no.l, which is a department of Civil Defence run by Government of 
India and for that regular recruitment procedure is provided. Workman cannot seek backdoor entry into service. 
Moreover, workman is not employee of respondent no.| being employee of respondent no.2 (contractor). 


23. In view of above discussion, it is held that since respondent no.2 (contractor) is currently not working with 
respondent no., so keeping in view the tenure of service rendered by the workman and salary given to him during the 
period of his stay with the contractor and non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act, this Tribunal is of the considered 
opinion that workman is entitled for compensation. 


24. Keeping in view the fact and circumstances of the present case, the following scheme of compensation is 
deemed fit by this Tribunal: 


Workman who worked for less than 2 years with contractor shall be entitled for Rs.20,000/-. 


il. Workman who worked for more than 2 years but less than 5 years with contractor shall be entitled 
Rs.30,000/-. 

ili. Workman who worked for more than 5 years with contractors shall be entitled for Rs.50,000/-. 

25. Present workman employed on 0.09.20i2 and was terminated on 27.0.20i8 (more than 5 years), so he is 

entitled for Rs.50,000/-. 

26. Respondent no.2 is directed to pay the workman Rs.50,000/- within one month from the date of the 


notification of the award failing which the respondent no.2 shall further pay interest @6% per annum from the date of 
award till the date of making payment. It is also added here that in case respondent no.| requires safai karamcharis, 
then workman may be engaged through any contractor on sympathetic ground.

3) Whether the principal employer pays the salary instead of contractor and

petition of the workman. In fact, claim petition is totally silent regarding the payment of wages, salary, letter of 
appointment by respondent no.! or by contractor or anything likewise. Thus, this basic feature for holding the

responsible to give notice to the conservancy staff provided by him. Respondent no.! has no roll in terminating the 
services of the workman. Thus, it was the respondent no.2 who was required to ensure the payment of wages to the 
workers engaged by him from time to time.

paid salary by the contractor and he was being controlled and supervised by the contractor. Thus, there does not exist 
any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.|. However, there exists relation 
of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.2.

(Regulation and Abolition) Act, 970 (hereinafter called as Contract Act), respondent no.2 was supplying contract 
labour to the respondent no.l. Thus, respondent no.2 would fall under the definition of contractor. Section 2(c) of the 
Contract Act is reproduced as under:

establishment, other than a mere supply of goods or articles of manufacture to such establishment, through contract 
labour or who supplies contract labour for any work of the establishment and includes a sub-contractor;

FLR 266 dealt at length with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in Section 2(j) of the Act, and

element is commercial (c) for the production or distribution of goods and services to calculated to satisfy human 
wants and wishes prima facie is an “Industry” in that enterprise. The workman was doing work i.e. systematic activity 
for respondent no.| at the asking of respondent no.2 and there was cooperation between the workman and respondent 
no.2, which involve substantial commercial element for rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, respondent 
no.2 would be termed as industry.

the Act. He also stated that he was appointed on 28.0.20l6 and he was paid minimum wages prescribed by Central

employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one 
employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty

activity for respondent no.| at the asking of respondent no.2 and there was cooperation between the workman and 
respondent no.2, which involve substantial commercial element for rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, 
respondent no.2 would be termed as industry. 


9. Workman in her deposition has clearly stated that there was non-compliance of Section 25F, 25G and 25H of 
the Act. She also stated that she was appointed on 02.0!.205 and she was paid minimum wages prescribed by 
Central Government and was working with respondent no.l. She was not given any compensation before terminating 
his services on 27.l0.208. In his cross examination, she has further stated that her salary used to be credited in his 
bank account. But she has not placed on record any bank account, in which her salary was credited in order to enable 
this Court to see who was making payment to the workman. However, there is no denial that the workman was paid 
salary by respondent no.2 (contractor). However, from the agreement dated 05.07.20I8 (Ex.R-2) placed on file by 
respondent no.l, it emerges that safai karamcharis were provided by respondent no.2 (contractor) to work with 
respondent no.l. Thus, workman was employee of respondent no.2 and not of respondent no.! as has been discussed 
above. There does not exist any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.|. 
However, there exists relation of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.2. 


20. Admittedly, there is non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2. However, as regards 
violation of other provisions i.e. Section 25G and 25H of the Act, there is no evidence lead by the workman. Hence, 
workman is entitled for compensation from respondent no.2. 


2i. It is also added here that there is no iota of evidence that any unfair labour practice used by respondent no.| 
by entering into contract with contractors for supply of safai karamcharis and agreement executed between respondent 
no.! and 2 cannot be said to be any unfair labour practice. So far as contentions of AR for workman that the work 
performed by the workman is of perennial in nature and no domestic inquiry was held before terminating the services 
of workman are concerned, in this regard, it is pointed out that workman was entitled only for compensation under 
Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2 (contractor) and no domestic inquiry was required to be conducted. Merely 
because work is of perennial in nature does not mean that any right has accrued in favour of the workman to get 
employment with respondent no.l, which is a department of Civil Defence run by Government of India and for that 
regular recruitment procedure is provided. Workman cannot seek backdoor entry into service. Moreover, workman is 
not employee of respondent no.|! being employee of respondent no.2 (contractor). 


22; In view of above discussion, it is held that since respondent no.2 (contractor) is currently not working with 
respondent no., so keeping in view the tenure of service rendered by the workman and salary given to him during the 
period of his stay with the contractor and non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act, this Tribunal is of the considered 
opinion that workman is entitled for compensation. 


23. Keeping in view the fact and circumstances of the present case, the following scheme of compensation is 
deemed fit by this Tribunal: 


i. Workman who worked for less than 2 years with contractor shall be entitled for Rs.20,000/-. 

il. Workman who worked for more than 2 years but less than 5 years with contractor shall be entitled 
Rs.30,000/-. 

ili. Workman who worked for more than 5 years with contractors shall be entitled for Rs.50,000/-. 

24. Present workman employed on 02.0!.20i5 and was terminated on 27.!0.20l8 (more than 2 years and less 


than 5 years), so she is entitled for Rs.30,000/-.

Findings:- 

3. The first contention regarding the applicant is that whether applicant comes within the definition of workman 
as is defined in Section 2(s) of the Act. I may mention that applicant was appointed as sweeper as per his claim 
petition and affidavit submitted before the Tribunal. In plain words the applicant was performing his duties as 
labourer/unskilled worker. He was not in supervisory or administrative post requiring him to perform only 
administrative duties. While interpreting Section 2(s) Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Devinder Singh Vs. 


Municipal Council, Sanaur, AIR 20I] Supreme Court 2532,has observed as follows:- 


“The source of employment, the quantum of recruitment, the terms & conditions of employmen?/ contract of 
service, the quantum of wages/ pay and mode of payment are not at all relevant for deciding whether or not a 
person is a workman within the meaning of Section 2(s) of the Act. The definition of workman also does not 
make any distinction between full time and part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. 
There is nothing in the plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be inferred that only person 
employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one 
employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty 
for fixed hours is not a workman.” 


4. Thus Hon’ble Supreme Court has clarified that the definition of workman also does not make any distinction 
between full time or part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is nothing in plain language of 
Section 2(s) from which it can be infer that only person employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing 
whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a 
casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a workman. In view of the ratio of law enunciated in the 
above ruling, in my considered opinion the applicant herein admittedly falls within the definition of ‘workman’ under 
Section 2(s) of the Act. 


5. The Hon’ble Supreme Court after analyzing the catena of cases has laid down in Balwant Raj Saluja Vs. Air 
India Limited in Civil Appeal ७०.70266 dated 25.06. 207/4, two well recognized tests to find out whether the labours 
are the contract employees of the principal employer are:- 


3) Whether the principal employer pays the salary instead of contractor and 
2) Whether the principal employer controls and supervise the work of the employees? 


6. The facts regarding the payment of salary by the management or contractor has not been stated in the claim 
petition of the workman. In fact, claim petition is totally silent regarding the payment of wages, salary, letter of 
appointment by respondent no.!l or by contractor or anything likewise. Thus, this basic feature for holding the 
relationship of employer and employee i.e. between respondent no.! and workman totally lacking not in the pleading 
but also in the evidence submitted by the workman.However, MWI Colonel K P Singh in his cross examination has 
stated that it is responsibility of the contractor to pay monthly wages to the conservancy staff provided by him. 
Respondent no.l has nothing to do with the minimum wages, DC rate to the conservancy staff. Contractor is 
responsible to give notice to the conservancy staff provided by him. Respondent no.! has no roll in terminating the

any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.l. However, there exists relation 
of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no. 2.

“Contractor”, in relation to an establishment, means a person who undertakes to produce a given result for the

9. The Hon’ble Apex Court in the case of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board Vs. A. Rajappa 
2928(36) FLR 266 dealt at length with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in Section 2(j) of the

is where (a) systematic activity (b) organized by cooperation between employer and employee (the direct and 
substantial element is commercial (c) for the production or distribution of goods and services to calculated to satisfy 
human wants and wishes prima facie is an “Industry” in that enterprise. The workman was doing work i.e. systematic 
activity for respondent no.| at the asking of respondent no.2 and there was cooperation between the workman and 
respondent no.2, which involve substantial commercial element for rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, 
respondent no.2 would be termed as industry.

2]. However, as regards violation of other provisions i.e. Section 25G and 25H of the Act, there is no evidence

Section 2(p) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 947 as follows:- 


(p) "settlement" means a settlement arrived at in the course of conciliation proceeding and includes a written 
agreement between the employer and workmen arrived at otherwise than in the course of conciliation proceeding 
where such agreement has been signed by the parties thereto in such manner as may be prescribed and a copy thereof 
has been sent to an officer authorised in this behalf by the appropriate Government and the conciliation officer; 


Section 8() provides as follows:- 
46, Persons on whom settlements and awards are binding. 


- [[२) A settlement arrived at by agreement between the employer and Workman otherwise than in the course of 
conciliation proceeding shall be binding on the parties to the agreement.

was to be in force upto 30th June /966 and the next settlement, incorporating practically the same terms, was again

settlements are under Section /6(//). 


4, Now the Authority constituted under Section 47(/) of the Act is an authority with very limited jurisdiction. It can 
only decide in the first appeal whether a termination by the management is valid or not and is within the parameters 
of Section 40 of the Act. The said Authority, in our view, has absolutely no jurisdiction to decide whether a settlement 
entered into under Section /6(7) of the Industrial Disputes Act between the representatives of the Workmen and of the 
Management, is vitiated by undue influence or misrepresentation or coercion on the part of the Management. The 
Authority, namely, the Assistant Commissioner of Labour, was never intended by the A.P. Legislature to have 
jurisdiction to go into the question of the validity of a settlement arrived at under Section /6 of the Industrial Disputes

Act, with extensive powers cannot be disputed. What we mean to say is that the Authority under Section 47(4) of the 
A.P. Act has no jurisdiction what-so-ever either to question or to decide about the validity of any such settlements. If 
parties to a settlement have a grievance about the validity of a settlement, it is for them to agitate the matter before 
the appropriate forum and they cannot ask an Authority constituted under Section 47/(/) of the A.P. Shops and 
Establishments Act, /966 with limited jurisdiction, to go into any such question and, that too, incidentally while 
deciding whether retirement as per the contract of employment, is legal or not.”

Further in the case of Herbertsons Limited Vs. Workmen of Herbertsons Limited and Ors, 4977 AIR 322,

The Tribunal thought that the question of the quantum of membership of the 2nd Respondent did not call for a finding 
at all in view of Ihis Court's order. As observed above that was not a correct assumption. On the other hand, we feel 
that this view of the Tribunal has led it to approach the matter in an entirely erroneous manner. The Tribunal is, 
rightly enough, conscious that under section 76 (/) of the Industrial Disputes Act the settlement was binding on the 
company and the members of the 3rd Respondent union. Even so, the Tribunal devoted nearly half of its order in 
scanning the evidence given by the company and Respondent No. 3 to find out whether the terms of the settlement had 
been explained by the President of the union to the workmen or not and whether the workers voluntarily accepted the 
settlement knowing all the "consequences". This to our mind is again an entirely wrong approach. 


“When a recognised union negotiates with an employer the workers as individuals do not come into the picture. It is 
not necessary that each individual worker should know the implications of the settlement since a recognised union, 
which is expected to protect the legitimate interests of labour, enters into a settlement in the best interests of labour. 
This would be the normal rule. We cannot altogether rule out exceptional cases where there may be allegations of 
mala fides, fraud or even corruption or other induce- ments. Nothing of that kind has been suggested against the 
President of the 3rd Respondent in this case. That being the position, prima facie, this is a settlement in the course of 
collective bargaining and, therefore, is entitled to due weight and consideration. 


It is not possible to scan the settlement in bits and pieces and hold some parts good and acceptable and others bad. 
Unless it can be demonstrated that the objectionable portion is such that it completely outweighs all the other 
advantages gained the Court will be slow to hold a settle- ment as unfair and unjust. The settlement has to be 
accepted or rejected as a whole and we are unable to reject it as a whole as unfair or unjust. Even before this Court 
the 3rd Respondent representing admittedly the large majority of the workmen has stood by this settlement and that is 
a strong factor which it is difficult to ignore. As stated elsewhere in the judgment, we cannot also be oblivious of the 
fact that all workmen of the company have accepted the settlement. Besides, the period of settlement has since expired 
and we are informed that the employer and the 3rd Respondent are negotiating another settlement with further 
improvements. These factors, apart from what has been stated above, and the need for industrial peace and harmony 
when a union backed by a large majority of workmen has accepted a settlement in the course of collective bargaining 
have impelled us not to interfere with this settlement. That being the position, we unhold the settlement as fair and just 
and order that the award of the Tribunal shall be substituted by the settlement dated October 6, /973, The said 
settlement shall be the substituted award. The appeal is disposed of accordingly. There will be no order as to costs.”

In order to prove the fact of 240 days of service within !2 months of a calendar year just preceding from the date of

Further, how to calculate 240 days of service by the Workman ina calendar year. In this context the reference of

In Rajasthan State Ganganagar S. Mills Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan and Anr. (2004) Apex Court held: 


"It was the case of the Workman that he had worked for more than 240 days in the year concerned. This claim was 
denied by the appellant. It was for the claimant to lead evidence to show that he had worked for 240 days in the year

In the case of Manager, RBI, Bangalore vs. S Mani (2005) SCC Page 00, the 3 Judges Bench of the Apex

“4, We have already extracted section 25B since its amendment and the change in language is the legislative

"These changes brought about by Act 36 of /964 appear to be clearly designed to provide that a Workman who has

42. In this context the reference of the decision of Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Oil and Natural Gas 
Corporation vs Krishan Gopal 2020(3) SCALE 272, date of decision 7.2.2020 is relevant therein Hon’ble 
Supreme Court have has laid down principle regarding regularization of the Workman on permanent posts. Hon’ble 
Supreme Court have laid down the prepositions of regularization of the workmen to permanent post is as under:- 


“(i) Wide as they are, the powers of the Labour Court and the Industrial Court cannot extend to a direction to order 
regularisation, where such a direction would in the context of public employment offend the provisions contained 
in Article /4 of the Constitution; 


(ii) The statutory power of the Labour Court or Industrial Court to grant relief to workmen including the status of 
permanency continues to exist in circumstances where the employer has indulged in an unfair labour practice by not 
filling up permanent posts even though such posts are available and by continuing to employ workmen as temporary 
or daily wage employees despite their performing the same work as regular workmen on lower wages; 


(iii) The power to create permanent or sanctioned posts lies outside the judicial domain and where no posts are 
available, a direction to grant regularisation would be impermissible merely on the basis of the number of years of 
service; 


(iv) Where an employer has regularised similarly situated workmen either in a scheme or otherwise, it would be open 
to workmen who have been deprived of the same benefit at par with the workmen who have been regularised to make 
a complaint before the Labour or Industrial Court, since the deprivation of the benefit would amount to a violation of 
Article /4, and 


(v) In order to constitute an unfair labour practice under Section 2(ra) read with Item 709 of the Vth Schedule of the 
ID Act, the employer should be engaging workmen as badlis, temporaries or casuals, and continuing them for years, 
with the object of depriving them of the benefits payable to permanent workmen. 


Thus, in view of the principles laid down by the Hon’ble Supreme Court as discussed above, in the instant matter the 
Workman utterly failed to prove his claim by adducing any documentary or oral evidence that the employer has 
indulged in unfair labour practice by not filling the permanent posts even though such posts are available and by 
continuing to employ workmen as temporary or daily wage employees despite their performance was the same work, 
as regular workmen on lower wages.

In the case of Mahboob Deepak vs. Nagar Panchayat Gajraula & Anr, Civil Appeal No.5875/2007 date of

“8. Respondent is a Local Authority. The terms and conditions of employment of the employees are governed by a 
Statute and statutory rules. No appointment can be made by a Local Authority without following the provisions of the 
recruitment rules. Any appointment made in violation of the said rules as also the constitutional scheme of equality as 
contained in Articles /4 and /6 of the Constitution of India would be a nullity. 


9. Due to some exigency of work, although recruitment on daily wages or on an ad hoc basis was permissible, but by 
reason thereof an employee cannot claim any right to be permanently absorbed in service or made permanent in 
absence of any statute or statutory rules. Merely because an employee has completed 240 days of work in a year 
preceding the date of retrenchment, the same would not mean that his services were liable to be regularized.”

In the case of F.C.I., vs. Kamdhenu Cattle Feed Industries 993 (I) SCC 7], therein Hon’ble Supreme Court have

“7. In contractual sphere as in all other State actions, the State and all its instrumentalities have to conform to Article 
_4 of the Constitution of which non-arbitrariness is a significant facet. There is no unfettered discretion in public law: 
A public authority possesses powers only to use them for public good. This impose the duty to act fairly and to adopt 
a procedure which is ‘fairplay in action’. Due observance of this obligation as a part of good administration raises a 
reasonable or legitimate expectation in every citizen to be treated fairly in his interaction with the State and its 
instrumentalities, with this element forming a necessary component of the decision making process in all State 
actions. To satisfy this requirement of non- arbitrariness in a State action, it is, therefore, necessary to consider and 
give due weight to the reasonable or legitimate expectations of the persons likely lo be affected by the decision or else 
that unfairness in the exercise of the power may amount to an abuse or excess of power apart from affecting the bona 
fides of the decision in a given case. The decision so made would be exposed to challenge on the ground of 
arbitrariness. Rule of law does not completely eliminate discretion in the exercise of power, as it is unrealistic, but 
providers for control of its exercise by judicial review.”

Section 2(p) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 947 as follows:- 


(p) "settlement" means a settlement arrived at in the course of conciliation proceeding and includes a written 
agreement between the employer and workmen arrived at otherwise than in the course of conciliation proceeding 
where such agreement has been signed by the parties thereto in such manner as may be prescribed and a copy thereof 
has been sent to an officer authorised in this behalf by the appropriate Government and the conciliation officer; 


Section 8() provides as follows:- 
46, Persons on whom settlements and awards are binding. 


- (२) A settlement arrived at by agreement between the employer and Workman otherwise than in the course of 
conciliation proceeding shall be binding on the parties to the agreement.

aforesaid settlements are binding on the parties to the agreement. The Learned Counsel for Workman has argued that

appointment basing on their seniority in terms of settlements entered between the Bank and the union..... Further, 
witness states that, “I am not having any document to show that any of my juniors are continuing in service.” 


Thus, from the above statement of the Workman witness WW it is clear that the panel was prepared in terms of 
various settlements entered into between Staff Federation of State Bank of India and State Bank of India and it was 
prepared on the basis of number of days of work put in by the temporary employees. Further, the Workman himself 
admitted that some of the temporary employees whose names were included in the panel were given regular 
appointment in the bank in order of their seniority in the panel and he is not having any document to show that any 
person who worked for less number of days than the Workman was given appointment in the bank. Therefore, the 
allegation of the Workman that the regular appointment has been made by the bank from the panel list in breach of 
the terms of the settlement and violation of seniority of panel list is not proved by this evidence of WWI. Thus, 
there is no evidence on record that bank has given the appointment to the temporary employees as well as daily 
wagers from the panel list [989 and 992 in breach of seniority of the temporary employees in the list. There is no 
evidence of jumbling in the panel list to make appointment of any permanent Workman in breach of the seniority. 
Therefore, I am constrained to hold that the Respondent Management has appointed the workmen from panel list in 
order of seniority and there is no jumbling of workmen in the panel list before it got lapsed on 3.3.997. 


40. However, Workman has taken the plea that the panels of Workmen for absorption in the employment of the 
Respondent banks (panels of temporary employees and daily wagers) has been lapsed on 3.3.997 in contravention 
of terms of settlement as the object of preparing the entire empanelment of temporary and daily wagers was to 
provide them permanent employment and till the both the panel lists exhausted the panel list cannot be lapsed on 
3.3.997 and the date of lapsing of the panel on 3.3.[997 has been fixed by the Respondent arbitrarily without any 
authority. 


4l. In this context, the perusal of Settlement dated 30.7.996 reveals that the 5 ॥ Settlement dated 30.7.996 
was entered under Section 2(p) and l8(/) of I.D. Act, 947 read with Rule 58 of Industrial Dispute (Central) Rules 
957. This settlement has been entered into by the competent parties and in this settlement parties thereto agreed 
that both the panels of temporary employees and daily wagers/casual employees will lapse on 3!.3.997. Thus the 
date of lapse of panel was fixed by both the parties with consensus under the settlement dated 30.7.996 and same is 
binding upon the Workman under the provision of Section 8(.) of I.D. Act, !947. Moreover, this issue of binding 
force of the settlement dated 7..987, 6.7.988, 27.0.988 and 9.!.99! has already been discussed, decided at 
finding in Point No.I of this award. However, the legality and validity of the aforementioned settlement has not been 
challenged by the Workman before any competent forum. Thus, claim of Workman that the date of lapse of panel 
i.e., 3.3.997 has been fixed arbitrarily by the Respondent bank is untenable. As regard the claim of Workman for 
his absorption to the permanent post it is settled law that the Workman can not claim his regularization to permanent 
post merely on the basis of number of working days. 


42. In this context the reference of the decision of Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Oil and Natural Gas 
Corporation vs Krishan Gopal 2020(3) SCALE 272, date of decision 7.2.2020 is relevant therein Hon’ble 
Supreme Court have has laid down principle regarding regularization of the Workman on permanent posts. Hon’ble 
Supreme Court have laid down the prepositions of regularization of the workmen to permanent post is as under: - 


“(i) Wide as they are, the powers of the Labour Court and the Industrial Court cannot extend to a direction to order 
regularisation, where such a direction would in the context of public employment offend the provisions contained 
in Article ॥4 of the Constitution; 


(ii) The statutory power of the Labour Court or Industrial Court to grant relief to workmen including the status of 
permanency continues to exist in circumstances where the employer has indulged in an unfair labour practice by not 
filling up permanent posts even though such posts are available and by continuing to employ workmen as temporary 
or daily wage employees despite their performing the same work as regular workmen on lower wages; 


(iii) The power to create permanent or sanctioned posts lies outside the judicial domain and where no posts are 
available, a direction to grant regularisation would be impermissible merely on the basis of the number of years of 
service; 


4346 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MAY 6, 2026/VAISAKHA 26, 948 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


(iv) Where an employer has regularised similarly situated workmen either in a scheme or otherwise, it would be open 
to workmen who have been deprived of the same benefit at par with the workmen who have been regularised to make 
a complaint before the Labour or Industrial Court, since the deprivation of the benefit would amount to a violation of 
Article /4, and 


(v) In order to constitute an unfair labour practice under Section 2(ra) read with Item 79 of the Vth Schedule of the 
ID Act, the employer should be engaging workmen as badlis, temporaries or casuals, and continuing them for years, 
with the object of depriving them of the benefits payable to permanent workmen. 


Thus, in view of the principles laid down by the Hon’ble Supreme Court as discussed above, in the instant matter the 
Workman utterly failed to prove his claim by adducing any documentary or oral evidence that the employer has 
indulged in unfair labour practice by not filling the permanent posts even though such posts are available and by 
continuing to employ workmen as temporary or daily wage employees despite their performance was the same work, 
as regular workmen on lower wages. 


43. Respondent has contended that all the vacancies exist and arise upto 3.3. [997 has been filled up from the 
panel list in order of seniority and no vacancy exists or arises as on 3.3. [997 remained unfilled. Further, it is 
contended that as per terms of settlement the life of panel lists has been lapsed on 3].3.[997, hence, there is no 
occasion to extend the life of panel lists beyond 3[.3,[997, However, the workman failed to prove contrary by any 
evidence to the aforesaid contention of the Respondent that the vacancies were existing as on 3.3.997 and the 
workman was not given absorption to the permanent post in order of his seniority. It is settled law that the power to 
create permanent or sanctioned post lies outside the judicial domain and where no posts are available, a direction to 
grant regularization would be impermissible merely on the basis of the number of years of service. Therefore, the 
claim of the workman on this ground also not acceptable. 


44. Further, as per the of settlement, panel was prepared for absorption of the workmen on the permanent posts 
has already been lapsed on 3.3.997 and the vacancies existing and arising upto 3.2.994 and upto 3.3.997 as 
settlement dated 30.7.996 has been filled up from the panel by appointing the workmen as per seniority in the panel 
list. Workman witness ४५४] in his cross examination has himself admitted this fact that, some of the temporary 
employees whose names were included in the panel were given regular appointment in the bank in order of their 
seniority in the panel. The Workman failed to show that there was any breach of terms of settlement has been 
committed by the Respondent in appointment to permanent post from aforesaid panel list. 


45. As discussed in preceding paragraph of this Award, the life of the panel has not been extended beyond 
3.3.997, by any further settlement hence, the panel list in which name of the Workman was included got expired 
on 3.3.997. It is not the case of the Workman that Respondent has regularized similarly situated workmen either in 
the scheme or otherwise and the Workman has been deprived of same benefit on par with those workmen or the 
vacancies remained unfilled on the date of lapse of panels i.e., 3.3.!997, Industrial Tribunal has no jurisdiction to 
extend the date of lapse of panel i.e., 3!.3.997. This Tribunal can not order for regularization of workmen to the 
permanent post in contravention of the provision of Article 4 of the Constitution of India. 


In the case of Mahboob Deepak vs. Nagar Panchayat Gajraula & Anr, Civil Appeal No.5875/2007 date of 
judgement 3.2.2007, Hon’ble Supreme Court have held:- 


“8. Respondent is a Local Authority. The terms and conditions of employment of the employees are governed by a 
statute and statutory rules. No appointment can be made by a Local Authority without following the provisions of the 
recruitment rules. Any appointment made in violation of the said rules as also the constitutional scheme of equality as 
contained in Articles /4 and /6 of the Constitution of India would be a nullity. 


9. Due to some exigency of work, although recruitment on daily wages or on an ad hoc basis was permissible, but by 
reason thereof an employee cannot claim any right to be permanently absorbed in service or made permanent in 
absence of any statute or statutory rules. Merely because an employee has completed 240 days of work in a year 
preceding the date of retrenchment, the same would not mean that his services were liable to be regularized.” 


Therefore, in view of the law laid down by the Hon’ble Apex Court, the claim of the Workman for absorption merely 
on the basis of number of day of work in the Respondent bank Branch is not acceptable. As regard plea of the 
Workman that the Workman should have been given employment even after 3!.3.997 as temporary Workman, it is 
the discretion of Respondent to engage the Workman depending upon availability of work and this Tribunal can not 
direct the Respondent to engage the Workman in the absent of such rule/scheme. 


46. In view of principle laid down by Hon’ble Apex Court as discussed above, in the instant matter Workman 
utterly failed to establish the fact of rendering continuous service for a period of 240 days of service within a period 
of 2 calendar months commencing and coming backward from relevant date i.e., the date of retrenchment, if has he 
would be denied to be in continuous service for a period of one year. Therefore, the provision contained under 
Sec.25F of retrenchment is not applicable to Workman. 


Counsel for Workman has relied upon number of decisions of Hon’ble High Court and Hon'ble Supreme Court and 
few of them are discussed herein:-

In the case of F.C.I., vs. Kamdhenu Cattle Feed Industries 993 () SCC 7I, therein Hon’ble Supreme Court have 
held:- 


“7. In contractual sphere as in all other State actions, the State and all its instrumentalities have to conform to Article 
_4 of the Constitution of which non-arbitrariness is a significant facet. There is no unfettered discretion in public law: 
A public authority possesses powers only to use them for public good. This impose the duty to act fairly and to adopt 
a procedure which is ‘fairplay in action’. Due observance of this obligation as a part of good administration raises a 
reasonable or legitimate expectation in every citizen to be treated fairly in his interaction with the State and its 
instrumentalities, with this element forming a necessary component of the decision making process in all State 
actions. To satisfy this requirement of non- arbitrariness in a State action, it is, therefore, necessary to consider and 
give due weight to the reasonable or legitimate expectations of the persons likely lo be affected by the decision or else 
that unfairness in the exercise of the power may amount to an abuse or excess of power apart from affecting the bona 
fides of the decision in a given case. The decision so made would be exposed to challenge on the ground of 
arbitrariness. Rule of law does not completely eliminate discretion in the exercise of power, as it is unrealistic, but 
providers for control of its exercise by judicial review.” 


In the case of State Bank of India, R.O., Vijayawada vs. Industrial Tribunal, Hyderabad WP १४०.१०३/997, 
therein Hon’ble High Court have held, 


“Sri Krovvidi Narasimham, the learned counsel for the 2" respondent contends, supporting the award that it was a 
permanent vacancy and even though the 27 respondent was appointed on temporary basis, his services were not 
liable to be terminated and he was to be regularised into service on permanent basis. Shastry award warrants that no 
temporary appointment can be made to a permanent post. But the matter is now covered by two division bench 
judgements dated 26. //./966 in W.A. ४०. 7297 of /7966 and 25.6. /967 in W.A. No.270 of 7962, The ratio decided in the

In the case of State of Haryana and others vs. Piara Singh and others. 992 (4) SCC 8, therein Hon’ble

“49. If for any reason an adhoc or temporary employee is continued for a fairly long spell, the authorities must 
consider his case for regularization provided he is eligible and qualified according to the rules and his service record 
is satisfactory and his appointment does not run counter to the reservation policy of the state.”

of Workman.

Section 2(p) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 947 as follows:- 


(p) "settlement" means a settlement arrived at in the course of conciliation proceeding and includes a written 
agreement between the employer and workmen arrived at otherwise than in the course of conciliation proceeding 
where such agreement has been signed by the parties thereto in such manner as may be prescribed and a copy thereof 
has been sent to an officer authorised in this behalf by the appropriate Government and the conciliation officer; 


Section 8() provides as follows:- 
46. Persons on whom settlements and awards are binding. 


- (२) A settlement arrived at by agreement between the employer and Workman otherwise than in the course of 
conciliation proceeding shall be binding on the parties to the agreement. 


Therefore, in view of the provision contained u/s.l8 (l) I.D. Act, 947, terms and conditions enumerated in the 
aforesaid settlements are binding on the parties to the agreement. The Learned Counsel for Workman has argued that 
the Workman after going through the selection procedure has successfully been listed in the panel for appointment on 
the permanent basis in the Respondent management and the empanelled list has to be valid till last person in the

issued by Respondent management thereby the services of the Workman has been terminated and the said order is not

Respondent in the 5" settlement has mentioned the date i.e., 3.3.997 for lapse of empanel list which is illegal and

aforesaid 5" settlement, is arbitrary and illegal.

rightly enough, conscious that under section I8 (/) of the Industrial Disputes Act the settlement was binding on the

“When a recognised union negotiates with an employer the workers as individuals do not come into the picture. It is 
not necessary that each individual worker should know the implications of the settlement since a recognised union, 
which is expected to protect the legitimate interests of labour, enters into a settlement in the best interests of labour. 
This would be the normal rule. We cannot altogether rule out exceptional cases where there may be allegations of 
mala fides, fraud or even corruption or other induce- ments. Nothing of that kind has been suggested against the 
President of the 3rd Respondent in this case. That being the position, prima facie, this is a settlement in the course of 
collective bargaining and, therefore, is entitled to due weight and consideration.

Unless it can be demonstrated that the objectionable portion is such that it completely outweighs all the other

“4, We have already extracted section 25B since its amendment and the change in language is the legislative

"These changes brought about by Act 36 of 7964 appear to be clearly designed to provide that a Workman who has
